questions.prompt: A customer has three matching orders. How many rows does an inner join return for that customer?

choices.text: Three rows because each matching pair contributes a result.
One row because the customer primary key is unique.
Zero rows because more than one match makes the join ambiguous.
One row containing an automatically aggregated order array.

questions.explanation: A join emits matching pairs. A unique customer key does not collapse its three matching orders.

sources.title: Table Expressions
sources.claim: An inner join produces each matching row pair; a left join preserves unmatched left rows with NULL right values, and ON filtering precedes outer-row preservation while WHERE filters its result.

questions.prompt: A report counts customers after joining their orders. Why can COUNT(*) exceed the customer count?

choices.text: The join inserts copies into the customer table.
SQL counts only distinct primary keys automatically.
Foreign keys force every customer to have several orders.
Each matching order can contribute another joined row.

questions.explanation: Joined rows have a different grain from customers. Aggregate deliberately, or count distinct customer keys when that is the requirement.

sources.title: Table Expressions

questions.prompt: All customers must appear, with only paid orders attached. Where should the paid-order test go?

choices.text: In WHERE orders.status = paid after the left join.
In an INNER JOIN because it preserves unmatched customers.
In the LEFT JOIN ON condition alongside the customer key match.
In WHERE with the key match, because ON and WHERE are interchangeable for outer joins.

questions.explanation: The ON predicate determines qualifying matches; LEFT JOIN then preserves customers without a qualifying order.

questions.prompt: A LEFT JOIN is followed by WHERE orders.status = paid. What happens to customers without any order?

choices.text: They remain because WHERE filters matches but never NULL-extended rows.
They remain because NULL equals any supplied status value.
They are removed because that predicate does not evaluate true.
They remain because LEFT JOIN overrides every later filter.

questions.explanation: WHERE retains true predicates. A NULL right-side status does not satisfy equality with paid.

questions.prompt: Which predicate finds rows whose optional shipped_at column is NULL?

choices.text: shipped_at = NULL
shipped_at = an empty string
shipped_at <> NULL
shipped_at IS NULL

questions.explanation: IS NULL tests missing values; ordinary comparisons with NULL do not become true.

sources.title: Table Expressions
sources.claim: WHERE discards false or NULL conditions; unmatched outer-join fields are NULL and IS NULL can identify them.

questions.prompt: An order must reference an existing customer and cannot omit that reference. Which constraints express both requirements?

choices.text: A foreign key plus NOT NULL on customer_id.
CHECK customer_id > 0 alone.
An index on customer_id without any constraint.
UNIQUE on customer_id alone.

questions.explanation: The foreign key enforces the relationship; NOT NULL disallows omitting the key. Uniqueness, positivity and indexing do not establish both.

sources.title: Constraints
sources.claim: Primary keys require unique non-NULL values; foreign keys enforce referenced-row existence for non-NULL key values, and NOT NULL separately controls whether missing values are allowed.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe join multiplicity? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An inner join can emit multiple rows for one left row.
A unique key on the left guarantees exactly one output row per left row.
An inner join automatically groups all matches into an array.
Counting joined rows can overcount distinct left-side entities.
A cross join of N and M rows emits N plus M rows.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: every matching pair contributes. B: Incorrect: several right rows can match one key. C: Incorrect: aggregation must be requested. D: Correct: count at the intended entity grain. E: Incorrect: a cross join emits N times M pairs.

sources.title: Table Expressions
sources.claim: Inner joins emit matching pairs and cross joins emit the Cartesian product.

questions.prompt: Which filter-placement claims are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An ON restriction can exclude a right match while preserving its left row.
ON and WHERE restrictions are always interchangeable for a left join.
A right-side equality in WHERE always preserves unmatched left rows.
A right-side equality in WHERE can remove NULL-extended rows.
WHERE is evaluated on the joined table result.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: left preservation follows matching. B: Incorrect: outer preservation makes placement significant. C: Incorrect: NULL equality is not true. D: Correct: such rows fail the equality predicate. E: Correct: it filters the FROM result.

sources.title: Table Expressions
sources.claim: LEFT JOIN ON restrictions determine matches before unmatched rows are preserved; WHERE restrictions then filter the joined result.

questions.prompt: Which NULL-handling statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A NULL right-side field always proves the left row itself is absent.
A comparison returning unknown is retained by WHERE like true.
A WHERE predicate must evaluate true for a row to remain.
NULL equals NULL under ordinary SQL equality.
IS NULL explicitly tests whether a value is missing.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: left joins preserve left rows with missing right fields. B: Incorrect: unknown does not satisfy WHERE. C: Correct: false and unknown are discarded. D: Incorrect: ordinary NULL comparison yields unknown. E: Correct: IS NULL is the missing-value predicate.

sources.title: Table Expressions
sources.claim: WHERE removes false or NULL results, and outer joins supply NULL values for unmatched right columns.

questions.prompt: Which constraint claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A NOT NULL constraint can prohibit an omitted customer reference.
A primary key permits duplicates if an application validates them first.
A foreign key can enforce that a supplied customer key exists.
A primary key combines uniqueness with a non-NULL requirement.
A foreign key alone necessarily requires a non-NULL reference.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: this is distinct from referential checking. B: Incorrect: duplicate primary keys violate the constraint. C: Correct: referenced-key existence is enforced. D: Correct: both properties define a primary key. E: Incorrect: nullable references can be permitted.

sources.title: Constraints
sources.claim: Primary keys require unique non-NULL values; foreign keys enforce referenced-row existence for non-NULL key values, and NOT NULL separately controls whether missing values are allowed.
